lines.text: Six minutes from the surface of the Moon, the computer landing Apollo Eleven began to fail.
July twentieth, nineteen sixty-nine. Eagle is falling toward the Sea of Tranquility.
Two men inside. Neil Armstrong. Buzz Aldrin.
Then a yellow light, and a number on the display.
Twelve oh two.
Armstrong radios Houston. Program alarm. It's a twelve oh two.
Nobody in the cockpit knew what it meant.
Six hundred million people were watching on Earth.
And in Houston, a twenty-six-year-old had seconds to decide: land, or abort.
The Apollo Guidance Computer was built at the M I T Instrumentation Laboratory.
It had about four kilobytes of working memory.
Its programs were woven by hand into copper rope.
And it was flying a spacecraft.
Its software team was led by Margaret Hamilton.
They had built it to expect trouble.
But that night, the trouble came from somewhere nobody had tested.
A radar switch, set for a possible abort, was flooding the computer with meaningless signals.
Each one stole a sliver of its time.
About fifteen percent, gone.
The computer was running out of room to think.
It restarted, threw away its least important jobs, and kept the ones that flew the ship.
The alarm was not a crash.
It was the computer saying: I'm overloaded, but I'm coping.
In Houston, guidance officer Steve Bales turned to his backroom.
Jack Garman, twenty-four, knew every alarm code.
If it doesn't keep happening, we're fine.
Bales made the call. We're go on that alarm.
It came back. Twelve oh one. Twelve oh two. Five alarms in all.
Then Armstrong saw the computer steering them toward a field of boulders.
He took manual control and flew on.
Eagle touched down with less than a minute of fuel left.
The Eagle has landed.
Margaret Hamilton received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in twenty sixteen.
Its code is public now. People are still finding bugs in it.
The software that landed on the Moon wasn't perfect.
It was built to survive being wrong.
